title: The flapper age and Harlem as playground of the world
summary: McRae says the 1920s were great: the charleston, the radio, and Harlem as the showplace where everybody came, from the Savoy to Connie's Inn.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Cabarets, honky-tonks and the Storyville nightlife scene

blocks.x: Well, just looking back on the 1920's, we often hear the 1920's as the age of the flapper, great changes, and certainly radio (of)
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
was on the scene and recording techniques.
Some of the things that you saw, were there -- was the flapper really all that the flapper had been made out to be?
Yeah, it was. It was a great year. The music was great, you know. All the music in those days was really --
People danced differently. They did the charleston and all that stuff, you know. That was a great thing, the charleston. (Inaudible) big band on the charleston.
Everybody loved to do it, (inaudible) the charleston. The breakdown, and all the different dances, you know.
And those things were just what they were supposed to be. It was a great year. That's when Harlem was like a --
Harlem was the showplace of the world. People came from all over to come to Harlem. Used to walk around Harlem all day.
I remember John Hammonds -- you know, he used to walk. He was (writing inaudible), you know. He
used to go the Savoy Ballroom, Paradise -- Small's Paradise, Connie's Inn. He'd walk all around the Rhythm Club.
He'd go all over Harlem. Nobody - Harlem was the playground of the world, you know. Everybody came to Harlem.
That song that Duke wrote, "Drop Me Off In Harlem," well that was true. That was a really true thing, because people just loved to come to Harlem.
